items.title: Filipino Singer Carmelle Storms to Victory in Eurovision Asia Debut in Bangkok
items.summary:
Filipino singer Carmelle won the first Asian edition of the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday (Nov. 14) with a fiery performance of her dance-pop song “Sobra-Sobra.”

Related

The 19-year-old beat 10 other acts in the grand final in Bangkok, with the winner chosen through votes from national juries in participating countries and viewers worldwide.

After her victory, Carmelle said her song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as “a tribute to all Filipino women.”

“I made history, since this was the first time,” she told The Associated Press . “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.”

Thai duo Mang x Daou finished second with an energetic performance of the romantic pop song “Aroma.” Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên placed third with a lively, stylish rendition of “Em Tiên.”

Malaysia’s Aina Abdul took fourth with her powerful ballad “Bluest Sky.” Thinla of Laos finished fifth with “Bae,” a playful dance track that had the audience dancing whenever it was replayed during the show.

Bhutan, South Korea, Mongolia, Nepal, Cambodia and Bangladesh also competed.

Contestants made their entrances aboard tuk-tuks, the motorized three-wheeled vehicles common in Bangkok’s tourist districts. They waved national flags as thousands of fans cheered inside the city-center venue.…

items.title: Richard Sterban, Oak Ridge Boys Bass Singer Who Helped Make ‘Elvira’ a Hit, Dies at 83
items.summary:
Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist behind the “oom poppa, mow mow” hook on one of The Oak Ridge Boys ‘ biggest hits, “Elvira,” and whose career launched as a backing singer for Elvis Presley , died on Saturday (Nov. 14). He was 83.

Related 

Gone But Not Forgotten: Musicians We Lost in 2026 

The Oak Ridge Boys’ Top 10 Billboard Hot Country Songs Hits 

The Oak Ridge Boys Member Richard Sterban Diagnosed With Pancreatic Cancer 

Sterban passed away due to complications from bronchitis and pneumonia in Hendersonville, Tenn., his family shared. He died after a long battle with cancer, and after retiring from touring last year.

“We appreciate all of your love, support, and prayers,” the Sterban family said in a statement released on Saturday. “Please continue to lift us up in this difficult time. We find comfort knowing that he is currently face to face with Jesus.”

Sterban, a member of The Oak Ridge Boys for more than 50 years with Duane Allen, William Lee Golden and the late Joe Bonsall, revealed a pancreatic cancer diagnosis in September 2025 , saying at the time that he was “under the care of the best cancer doctors in the country and, with the help of the Good Lord above, I believe I will be able to get through this.”

“Elvira” — The Oak Ridge Boys’ highest-charting single on the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, a song that became one of the quartet’s numerous No. 1s on the Hot Country Songs chart, and the winner of a trio of major awards (a Grammy Award, a CMA Award and an ACM Award) put Sterban’s deep vocal front and center in the hit’s chorus.

items.title: Karol G Surprises Mexico City Fans With Thalía as Special Guest: ‘The First Person I Wanted to Be’
items.summary:
Karol G gave her fans a huge surprise on Friday (Nov. 13) during the first of her three nights at the Estadio GNP Seguros in Mexico City, inviting Thalia to join her on stage for a special performance. The appearance of the iconic Mexican pop star, who had not performed in the capital for a decade, sent the audience into a frenzy.

“She was my first idol in life,” an emotional Karol G told the 65,000 concertgoers during her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour, according to promoter Ocesa. “The first person I wanted to be, when I dreamed of becoming a singer, was named Thalia, and she’s here with me tonight.”

Before Thalia appeared, a video was shown of a young Karol G saying that she wanted to be like her. The Mexican superstar then took to the stage wearing a replica of her iconic guitar-shaped bustier from her “Amor a la Mexicana” era — one of the most famous outfits in Latin pop culture. The new version of the outfit was decorated by Thalia herself, as she had teased a few days earlier in an Instagram post without revealing its purpose.

Together, they performed Thalia’s classics “Piel Morena” and “Amor a la Mexicana,” followed by “¿A Quién le Importa?” — a cover of the Spanish group Alaska y Dinarama’s hit, which Thalia reimagined in 2002. 

The singer and actress known for telenovelas like María la del Barrio and Marimar praised Karol G’s strength and resilience. “She doesn’t care what the world has to say about her,” Thalia said while singing the Alaska y Dinarama anthem, getting a roaring cheer from the audience as they celebrated the union of two stars from different…
items.t: Karol G Surprises Mexico City Fans With Thalía as Special Guest: ‘The First Person I Wanted to Be’

items.title: James Blunt: ‘Do I have a nickname? Yes, it rhymes with blunt’
items.summary:
The singer on his love for Ibiza, the weirdest thing he’s done in the name of romance, and being signed up for Celebrity Traitors against his will

You were a punching bag for such a long time after You’re Beautiful became a massive hit but your consistent good humour is deeply admirable. Does it ever get tiring?

It was a surprise, at the beginning. I was just a little guy with a dream. And when you achieve your dream, you think people would be happy for you. For them not to be happy for you but angry with you, for your song, seems irrational, an overreaction. It is interesting how people generally want to tear people down for achieving their little dreams. But I’d had a real proper job before that [as a captain in the British army]. My friends might have been on operations in Afghanistan or Iraq, so if I were to complain to them at the time saying, “Oh, the Guardian said something really horrid about me and gave me three stars for my album” – they would be able to talk about who had lost their lives or limbs that day, and that put it all in perspective. And perspective is everything.

items.title: Kate Nash to lose $16,000 from current tour as she keeps afloat with OnlyFans money
items.summary:
Kate Nash has said she expects to lose around $16,000 (£12,000) on her North American tour, and will continue posting content on OnlyFans to help cover the costs.

READ MORE: Kate Nash on OnlyFans, The Lottery Winners and saving the music industry: “Major labels are scared – and they should be” 

The ‘Foundations’ singer first joined the subscription platform in November 2024 as part of her ‘Butts For Tour Buses’ campaign , which aimed to highlight the financial pressures facing touring musicians.

Now, in a new video on her recently launched OnlyFans TV channel, Nash has said that the same problems persist as she tours the US in support of her forthcoming sixth album, ‘Cailín’.

“When I put out my record ‘9 Sad Symphonies’ in 2024, and I started touring it, I realised how much the grassroots of music and culture really was in crisis,” she explained.

items.title: U2’s The Edge breaks his silence on sequel to ‘Elf’

U2 ‘s The Edge has spoken out after an unlikely story emerged that he had written a sequel to Will Ferrell ‘s Christmas comedy Elf .

Earlier this month, comedian and actor Andy Richter revealed that the guitarist had written an unproduced follow-up to the 2003 film, directed by Jon Favreau.

Richter, who appeared in Elf as children’s author Morris, explained that the film’s producer Shauna Robertson had been contacted about the U2 guitarist’s proposed sequel, but the project ultimately went nowhere.

Now, The Edge has addressed the story himself in a new interview with CBS Sunday Morning .

“It’s an outrage for someone to suggest that I would write a script,” he joked. “I wrote a treatment – it’s a different thing – for my own amusement, yes.”

He explained that coming up with film ideas was something he had experienced several times in the past.

“This happened to me about three or four times. I will wake up, and I will have a complete movie outline in my head,” he said.

Recalling his idea for Elf 2 , he added: “This morning, I woke up with this idea in my head for a sequel to Elf .”

The guitarist said he was a huge fan of the original film and had written down his ideas before discussing them with a friend who worked as a film producer.

“I think I just shared it with a couple of people,” he explained. “Honestly, I thought it was so far-fetched that I didn’t take it terribly seriously. But you never know.”

items.title: Robyn says Eurovision is “just shit” now: “It really is embarrassing”
items.summary:
Robyn has delivered a scathing assessment of the Eurovision Song Contest , describing the competition as “just shit” and “embarrassing”.

READ MORE: The Big Read – Robyn: “I danced a lot on my own” 

The Swedish singer made the comments during an appearance on Amy Poehler ‘s Good Hang podcast, which was released on Tuesday (November 10).

Towards the end of their conversation, Poehler asked Robyn about the importance of Eurovision to European audiences, prompting the singer to laugh before giving her unfiltered opinion.

“We don’t have ABBA anymore, so I don’t really watch Eurovision,” she began. “They were one of the first people to win the whole thing for us, with ‘Waterloo’. Hard to beat.

“Then we had Carola; both me and Zara [Larsson] grew up listening to her. Amazing artist. Now, it’s just shit, I would say.”

Robyn continued: “I have American friends that I watch it with. My friend Bart has a blanket that he pulls up over his eyes while we’re watching ’cause it’s so embarrassing, and it really is embarrassing.

“And after I watched it, I feel really just overstimulated, and in a bad way. I was looking for words I’m not gonna say. But yeah, I don’t like it.”

Sweden has a particularly successful history at Eurovision, having won the contest seven times. ABBA’s victory with ‘Waterloo’ in 1974 helped launch their international career, while Carola Häggkvist claimed the trophy in 1991 with ‘Fångad av en stormvind’.

More recently, Loreen won the competition in 2012 with ‘Euphoria’ and again in 2023 with ‘Tattoo’, becoming only the second performer to win Eurovision…
items.t: Robyn says Eurovision is “just shit” now: “It really is embarrassing”

items.title: Noel Fielding breaks silence on Russell Brand after rape and sexual assault conviction
items.summary:
Noel Fielding has spoken out about Russell Brand following his conviction for rape and sexual assault, distancing himself from their past relationship and expressing regret over their jokes.

Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison on Monday (November 9) , having been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Fielding, who worked alongside Brand on numerous television, radio and live comedy shows during the 2000s, has now addressed their relationship in a statement to The Sun .

“I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand’s crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice,” he said.

“I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years.

“Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them.”

Fielding and Brand became familiar collaborators during the 2000s, appearing together on The Big Fat Quiz Of The Year , Brand’s BBC radio programmes and live comedy events.

They also performed together under the name The Goth Detectives, including at a Teenage Cancer Trust charity show at London’s Royal Albert Hall in 2013 , which was organised by Noel…
items.t: Noel Fielding breaks silence on Russell Brand after rape and sexual assault conviction

items.title: Rosalía makes history with Album Of The Year award win at Latin Grammys and performs ‘Lux’ medley
items.summary:
Rosalía has made history at the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards, winning Album Of The Year for the third time and playing a medley of songs from ‘Lux’ – watch below.

READ MORE: Rosalía live in London: a breathtakingly brilliant work of art 

The Spanish star was among the biggest winners at the 27th annual ceremony, which took place at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas last night (November 12).

She claimed the night’s biggest prize for ‘Lux (Complete Works)’, becoming the first woman to win Album Of The Year three times as a lead artist, following her previous victories for ‘El Mal Querer’ in 2019 and ‘Motomami’ in 2022.

The achievement places her alongside Alejandro Sanz and Juanes, who have also won the category three times. Only Juan Luis Guerra has won it more often, with four victories.

Rosalía was visibly emotional as she accepted the award from Juanes, recalling how the Colombian musician had supported her at the beginning of her career, attending concerts in Madrid when she was performing to audiences of around 100 people.

Addressing the audience in Spanish, she reflected on the creative risks behind her three award-winning albums.

“This is the third time I’ve won this award, and — just as ‘El Mal Querer’ felt like a dream, or ‘Motomami’ was a gamble — ‘Lux’ has been, for me, a leap into the void,” she said.

“I believe it’s very important to speak your own truth and for others to be able to speak theirs; this album is my truth.”

She also thanked the people who had supported her artistic vision, as well as reflecting on those who had previously dismissed her…
items.t: Rosalía makes history with Album Of The Year award win at Latin Grammys and performs ‘Lux’ medley

items.title: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month
items.summary:
(Erased Tapes)
Dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements, virtuosic vocals and echoes of PJ Harvey and Massive Attack make this disarming debut a one-of-a-kind creation

Since the release of her debut EP, Qasr, in 2024, south Asian-American vocalist and composer Sheherazaad has developed a distinctive take on the classical singing of her heritage. While her contemporaries such as the singers Ganavya and Manizeh draw on spiritual vocal traditions, and Arooj Aftab on jazz and folk instrumentation, Sheherazaad’s work is darker and far more introspective, using sparse acoustic arrangements to create a style of Urdu-language noir.

On this debut album, she delivers her most disarmingly eerie and mournful work yet. A heavy layer of reverb coats the record’s spare and often evocative arrangements, making undulating tabla hits echo beneath Sheherazaad’s keening vocals on Qatil, while on Registaan it lends an unnervingly distorted quality to a simple guitar refrain and on Mard it subsumes melody in a haze of resonance. The resulting atmosphere sits somewhere between PJ Harvey’s late-90s eerie grunge and the trip-hop qawwali of Massive Attack’s work with singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan – an ambience that is…
items.t: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month

Boris Kor Tom Zeebroek is staring up at a grey gothic building in the centre of Ghent, squinting through the late September sun that is covering his home town in a cloak of unseasonal warmth.

Zeebroek is encouraging his bandmate Charlotte Adigéry and I to crane our necks towards the Mammelokker, an 18th-century Flemish relief on the top of the building. It’s a gruesome bit of stone, which sits above the town square and depicts a daughter suckling her own father. The pair are taking me on a tour of their medieval home town, and this disturbing architectural decoration is part of our itinerary.

items.title: Hamlet Hail to the Thief could have been rotten but redeems Radiohead’s ‘record that got away’ | Alexis Petridis
items.summary:
The band’s uneven 2003 album has been judiciously reworked to accompany a staging of Shakespeare’s tragedy with quite extraordinary results

According to the programme notes, Thom Yorke had serious reservations about director Christine Jones’ idea to stage a production of Hamlet featuring music from Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief. Who can blame him? Many criticisms have been laid at Radiohead’s door but being hopelessly naff isn’t one of them, and, alas, naff is very much the adjective you’d apply to a lot of attempts to meld Shakespeare and rock music.

You’re often in the realm of high camp – portentous, Bard-quoting heavy metal lyrics; Return to the Forbidden Planet’s jokey blending of The Tempest with 50s rock’n’roll; 2015’s These Paper Bullets, which relocated Much Ado About Nothing to swinging London, complete with Beatle-y songs by Green Day’s Billie Joe Armstrong – or of buttock-clenching disasters like Catch My Soul, a 1971 rock adaptation of Othello which required Black American soul singer PP Arnold to star opposite impresario Jack Good, playing the title role in blackface.

items.title: ‘Joni Mitchell sang Both Sides, Now over the phone to me’: folk music legend Judy Collins on her 87 remarkable years
items.summary:
As she continues her farewell tour, the US singer-songwriter answers your questions on romance with Stephen Stills, friendship with Carly Simon and how folk underpins all pop

How did you come into Joni Mitchell’s orbit and how did you end up recording Both Sides, Now before she did? Steve-bayley
I’m 48 years sober, but in the old days I drank. One night in 1967, I was passed out and the phone rang at about 3am. It was my friend [the musician, songwriter and producer] Al Kooper. He said he’d been at a club and had run into this woman, Joni, who wrote songs. He put her on the phone and she sang Both Sides, Now over the phone. It was brilliant. I said: “I’ll be right over.” I recorded it the next day and it became a huge hit.

I don’t think Joni was too happy that I was the first to record it, but she was very generous and I’ve since recorded many of her songs. She was unknown then, so I’m proud that I was able to help introduce her to the world. She’s one of the great writers of all time.

items.title: Blackhaine: Saints in the Wethouse review | Alexis Petridis's album of the week
items.summary:
(XL Recordings)
His Playboi Carti collabs may have dragged Tom Heyes out of the underground, but this bracing debut remains far from the mainstream, full of garbled barks and walls of noise

On the second track on his debut album, Tom Heyes accuses lesser artists of copying him. “What the fuck you even take me for?” he barks on Northside Needs Me, over a grinding, distorted bassline that comes punctuated with stammering, rave-y vocal samples. “Too much noise shit, replicating what I played before.”

Of course, charging that others are merely imitating what you did previously is a venerable rap tradition: the track that gave said practice its longstanding name, Bite’n My Stylee by Original Concept, is now 40 years old. Perhaps it’s true that others have been copying the approach that Heyes has minted under the alias of Blackhaine, but if so, it seems faintly remarkable, because his approach is so determinedly unique.

items.title: ‘Young, Black and female in Brixton is hard’: ​from football to Top Boy and wordplay, the inspiring journey of UK rapper Cristale
items.summary:
Crystal Palace FC or Oxbridge beckoned, but the multitalented MC kept forging her way towards music. She explains how she poured every aspect of herself into her debut mixtape

Two weeks before we meet, UK rapper Cristale was scrambling down a cliff face to a secluded black pebbled beach in Dover, racing an incoming tide with fewer than 90 minutes to shoot the video for her single I’m Okay With Being Lonely. She’d never hiked before in her life. “I was wearing head-to-toe Stone Island, no hiking gear, full face of makeup, edges laid and Mum was doing my touch-ups on a rusty ladder,” she laughs.

As we sit in her publicist’s central London office, her hair half-braided and half-flowing past a black puffer coat, she says the rush of adrenaline hasn’t fully faded. In fact she seems to thrive on regular bumps of it: beyond her relentlessly articulate and energetic rap flow – put to work on tracks that span drill, introspective R&B and beyond – she has ably hopped between football, art, acting in Netflix projects and more.

items.title: ‘My partners would all tell you I was a nut job’: Jane Wiedlin on the Go-Go’s, fame and the freedom of sex dungeons
items.summary:
As she releases a brutally honest memoir, the new wave icon opens up about industry sexism, living with bipolar disorder and becoming ‘the world’s first atheist ordained minister’

The first thing Jane Wiedlin tells me before our interview even begins is that, an hour or so earlier, she downed two beers. “It keeps me cheerful,” she says with a laugh. The disclosure dovetails with the reason we’re doing the interview in the first place, which is to unpack her new memoir, a tome that deserves a truth-in-advertising award for its title alone: TMI (as in “too much information”). “I’ve always been TMI!” Wiedlin proudly announces. “I’m the one who always wanted to expose the truth. This book is my first opportunity to do so.”

A portion of that truth has to do with the band she helped form in the late 70s, the Go-Go’s. The five-piece are not only the first all-female band who play their own instruments and write their own material to earn a No 1 album in the US but, astonishingly, are the only such group to hold that distinction nearly 45 years later. The group’s power-pop music, heard in zippy hits like Our Lips Are Sealed and Vacation, led to their induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021, inspired a Broadway play and influenced modern female artists all the way from Olivia Rodrigo to Wet Leg.

items.t: ‘My partners would all tell you I was a nut job’: Jane Wiedlin on the Go-Go’s, fame and the freedom of sex dungeons
